ai.literal: As the way of conduct, let one adopt, in one's own mind, the nature of not having envy.
ai.translation: Let a person adopt as their very rule of conduct the state of mind that is entirely free from envy.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் தன் நெஞ்சத்தில் பொறாமை இல்லாத குணத்தையே தன் ஒழுக்க நெறியாகக் கொள்ள வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet teaches that the most fundamental rule of conduct a person can practice is keeping their mind free from envy. The word 'ஒழுக்காறு' refers to the path of righteous conduct, which is elevated here to mean a core life principle. By advising us to 'adopt' (கொள்க) this envy-free nature (இயல்பு) within our own heart (நெஞ்சத்து), the poet emphasizes that true virtue is an internal state of being. Eliminating jealousy from the mind is thus presented as the primary step toward a moral life.

ai.literal: Than excellent attainment, that-equal there is not, towards anyone, of envy, the absence, if one obtains.
ai.translation: If one can attain the state of being free from envy towards anyone, there is no greater attainment than that in life.
ai.modern: யாரிடத்தும் பொறாமை கொள்ளாத குணத்தைப் பெற்றால், அதைவிடச் சிறந்த பேறு வேறு எதுவும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the supreme value of overcoming jealousy. The poet states that if a person can obtain the quality of being free from envy (அழுக்காற்றின் அன்மை) towards anyone (யார் மாட்டும்), there is no greater fortune or attainment (விழுப்பேறு) than that. The word 'விழுப்பேறு' refers to a highly esteemed gain, and the couplet shows that mental purity and freedom from ill-will are the greatest wealth one can ever acquire.

ai.literal: Virtue (and) prosperity he who does not desire, is he who, another's prosperity not cherishing, envies.
ai.translation: He who does not rejoice in another's prosperity and envies them is one who desires neither virtue nor his own progress.
ai.modern: பிறருடைய வளர்ச்சியைப் போற்றாமல் பொறாமைப்படுபவன், அறத்தையும் தன் வளர்ச்சியையும் விரும்பாதவன் ஆவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the self-destructive nature of envy. The poet states that a person who cannot bear to see another's prosperity and envies them is equivalent to someone who does not desire virtue or personal growth for themselves. Envy is not just a passive feeling; it actively blocks one's own moral and material advancement. By begrudging the success of others, the envious person shuts the door on their own well-being.

ai.literal: Through envy, evil deeds they will not do, through the path of moral slip, ruin will befall, having known.
ai.translation: Those who clearly realize that ruin will inevitably befall them if they stray into wrongful paths do not commit evil deeds out of envy.
ai.modern: பொறாமை காரணமாக வரும் தவறான வழியால் தமக்குத் துன்பம் உண்டாகும் என்பதை உணர்ந்தவர்கள், பொறாமையினால் பிறருக்குத் தீமைகளைச் செய்ய மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights how wise people avoid the destructive nature of envy. The word 'அழுக்காறு' means envy, and 'அழுக்காற்றின்' refers to acting under its influence. 'இழுக்காறு' refers to a moral slip or deviation from the right path, while 'ஏதம்' means ruin or distress. The poet explains that those who understand ('அறிந்து') that straying into wrongful paths ('இழுக்காற்றின்') will inevitably bring ruin ('ஏதம் படுபாக்கு') upon themselves will never commit harmful deeds ('அல்லவை செய்யார்') out of envy.

ai.literal: To those who possess envy, that itself is sufficient; even if enemies fail to harm, it will yield ruin.
ai.translation: For those who harbor envy, that vice alone is sufficient to destroy them; even if their enemies fail to do them harm, envy itself will yield their ruin.
ai.modern: பொறாமை உடையவர்களுக்கு அந்தப் பொறாமை ஒன்றே போதுமானது; பகைவர்கள் தீங்கு செய்யத் தவறினாலும், அதுவே அவர்களுக்கு அழிவைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the self-destructive power of envy. For a person who possesses envy (அழுக்காறு உடையார்), no external enemies are required to bring about their downfall. Even if their enemies fail (வழுக்காயும்) to inflict harm, the envy itself is entirely sufficient (சாலும்) to yield (ஈன்பது) complete ruin (கேடு). The poet emphasizes that envy acts as an internal foe, making external adversaries redundant in causing one's destruction.

ai.literal: The family of him who envies that which is given will perish, without even clothing and food.
ai.translation: The family of one who envies the gifts given to others will perish, stripped of even basic clothing and food.
ai.modern: பிறருக்குக் கொடுப்பதைக் கண்டு பொறாமைப்படுபவனுடைய சுற்றத்தார், உடுத்துவதற்கும் உண்பதற்கும் கூட இல்லாமல் அழிந்து போவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the devastating consequences of harboring envy (அழுக்காறு) towards the charity or gifts given to others. The poet states that if a person feels jealous when someone gives a gift to another, it is not just that individual who suffers, but their entire family (சுற்றம்) that will face ruin. The ruin is so absolute that they will lack even the barest necessities of life: clothing (உடுப்பதூஉம்) and food (உண்பதூஉம்). The poetic lengthening (அளபெடை) in these two words emphasizes the extreme deprivation of these basic needs.

ai.literal: Having envied, him who has jealousy, the Goddess of Prosperity, her elder sister having shown, will leave.
ai.translation: The Goddess of Prosperity will turn away from a person who harbors envy, and pointing him out to her elder sister, the Goddess of Misfortune, she will abandon him.
ai.modern: பொறாமை கொண்டு அழுக்காறு உடையவனாக வாழ்பவனை, திருமகள் தன் மூத்தவளாகிய மூதேவிக்குக் காட்டிவிட்டு அவனிடமிருந்து நீங்கிவிடுவாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the destructive nature of envy by using the personified deities of wealth and poverty. The Goddess of Prosperity (Seyyavaḷ) cannot tolerate a person who harbors jealousy and grudges others' success. Instead of staying with such a person, she will point him out to her elder sister, the Goddess of Misfortune (Tavvai), and leave him in her hands. The contrast between 'Seyyavaḷ' and 'Tavvai' illustrates the complete reversal of fortune that awaits an envious person.

ai.literal: Envy called a sinner, wealth having destroyed, into an evil place having led, will cast.
ai.translation: The sinner called envy will utterly destroy a person's wealth and drive them into the path of misery.
ai.modern: பொறாமை என்று சொல்லப்படும் ஒரு பாவி, ஒருவனுடைய செல்வத்தை அழித்து, அவனைத் தீய வழியிலே செலுத்திவிடும்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, envy is personified as a destructive sinner. The poet warns that envy does not merely cause mental distress, but actively ruins a person's life in two ways. First, it destroys their existing prosperity and wealth. Second, it drives them into wretched situations or evil paths, represented by the term 'tīyuḻi' (evil place).

ai.literal: The prosperity of the envious-hearted person and the ruin of the upright person will be pondered.
ai.translation: The prosperity of an envious-hearted person and the adversity of an upright person are matters to be deeply pondered.
ai.modern: பொறாமை குணம் கொண்டவனுடைய செல்வமும், நேர்மையானவனுடைய வறுமையும் (மக்களால் வியப்புடன்) ஆராய்ந்து நினைக்கப்படும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet addresses a common paradox in human life: the prosperity of the wicked and the suffering of the righteous. The poet states that the wealth of an envious person (அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கம்) and the ruin of an upright person (செவ்வியான் கேடு) are anomalies that will be deeply pondered and analyzed by the world. Here, 'அவ்வியம்' refers to envy or crookedness of the mind, while 'செவ்வி' refers to rectitude or equity. By stating that these situations are 'to be pondered' (நினைக்கப்படும்), the poet implies that such unnatural states of fortune are temporary, unnatural, and bound to be resolved by the laws of nature.

ai.literal: Having rid of envy, those who prospered even, do not exist; that (envy) those who do not have, in prosperity, those who were ruined even, do not exist.
ai.translation: No one has ever prospered through envy, nor has anyone free from envy ever been ruined of their prosperity.
ai.modern: பொறாமை கொண்டு பெருமையடைந்தவர்களும் இல்லை; அந்தப் பொறாமை இல்லாதவர்களில் தம் செல்வச் செழிப்பை இழந்தவர்களும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute law of envy and its consequences on human fortune. The first part asserts that history has never seen anyone who truly grew great or prospered by harboring envy. Conversely, the second part states that those who are free from envy have never been ruined or deprived of their wealth. The contrast between 'அகன்றார்' (those who expanded or prospered) and 'தீர்ந்தார்' (those who were ruined or depleted) shows that envy never builds up, and the lack of envy never tears down.
